ch01.note: The Shinsengumi, the 'Newly Selected Corps,' was a band of swordsmen the Tokugawa shogunate licensed to police Kyoto in the last turbulent years of its rule. Formed in 1863, it was commanded by Kondō Isami with Hijikata Toshizō as its vice-commander, and this novel is its story, seen through Hijikata. At the point the narrative opens, in 1857, the corps still lies six years in the future, and the two men are only friends from neighboring farm villages.

A ri was about 3.9 kilometers, two and a half miles, so the two villages lay within some twelve kilometers of each other. The distances Toshizō covers in this chapter — two and a half ri to Fuchū, two ri to Hachiōji — are a couple of hours' walking apiece.

Ansei was a Japanese era name; its fourth year is 1857 in the Western calendar. Years were still reckoned by such era names, changed on the accession of an emperor or after some inauspicious event. Toshizō was then twenty-two.

The hachijūhachiya, the eighty-eighth night counted from the first day of spring in the old calendar — about the first of May. A marker of the farming year, the traditional time of the last frost and of the tea-picking, it fixes the action at the very start of summer.

Under the Tokugawa order, dress and hairstyle were badges of inherited class. A farmer's son wore the plain sukobin style; the shaved pate and oiled topknot of the warrior were not his to assume. For Toshizō, a peasant, to dress his hair in imitation of a samurai's was a small, deliberate insolence — of a piece with his boast that he would be a samurai one day, which in the event he became.

The nanushi was a village headman, the lowest office of Tokugawa rural administration: a leading farmer, not a samurai, who gathered the land tax and kept order for the domain. Satō Hikogorō (1827–1902), headman of nearby Hino, was married to Toshizō's elder sister and kept a fencing hall of the Tennen Rishin-ryū, the school Kondō would head; it was there the two trained. He remained Toshizō's kinsman and patron for life.

The Kurayami Matsuri, the great festival of the Ōkunitama Shrine at Fuchū, is still held every year from late April into early May. Its name — kurayami, darkness — comes from its central rite, the night procession of the shrine's mikoshi, once carried through streets with every lamp put out so the deity might pass unseen. The festival and its darkened procession are historical; the licentious free-for-all Shiba describes is the novel's dramatization of the old sense that the god's night stood outside ordinary rule, and should not be taken as documented custom.

The old day was divided into twelve two-hour periods named for the zodiac animals. The hour of the Dog ran roughly from seven to nine in the evening; the hour of the Rat, which sounds later in the chapter to open the procession, fell around midnight.

ch01.anchor: the daughter of a great Shinshū temple
ch01.note: Jōdo Shinshū, the True Pure Land school, is the one branch of Japanese Buddhism whose clergy have always married and raised families, so that a temple could have a daughter and descend in a hereditary line. Its lay followers are the monto, the parishioners named here, who by custom addressed the priest's daughter with the honorific rendered 'the young lady.'

Ishida sanyaku was a real patent remedy of the Hijikata house, sold for broken bones and bruises. The family made and peddled it from the early eighteenth century until Japan's postwar drug law ended it in 1948; Toshizō truly did hawk it on foot across the provinces, in the manner of the Toyama medicine sellers, with several hundred customers on his books. It was compounded from a riverside weed, charred and ground to powder and taken down in hot sake. Its efficacy, described so vividly in the next paragraph, is the tradition's own claim; the hot sake may have done as much as the powder.

A leap forward to 1864, seven years past the scene at hand. In the Ikedaya Affair the Shinsengumi stormed an inn in Kyoto and cut down a gathering of anti-shogunal loyalists — the exploit that made the corps famous. The novel reaches it in its course; here Shiba names it only to vouch for the medicine.

ch01.anchor: all shogunal domain and temple-and-shrine land
ch01.note: The Tama country west of Edo was held in fief by no warrior lord: it was tenryō, land administered directly for the shogun, together with estates belonging to temples and shrines. Because no samurai household was seated there, the district had, as the narrator says, no warrior families and no women of rank — which is the whole engine of Toshizō's frustrated craving for a high-born woman.

Yobai, 'night-crawling,' was a real custom of the old farming villages: a young man would slip into a girl's room after dark, and if he was welcome the match might be owned to later. The trick of wetting the wooden shutter-track, so it slides without its usual squeal, belongs to that lore. Shiba presents Toshizō's use of it, here and at the temple, as something colder than courtship.

Norishige of Etchū Province (early fourteenth century) was one of the great swordsmiths, counted among the ten disciples of the master Masamune and working in the Sōshū manner. His blades are prized for a swirling grain in the steel that connoisseurs call matsukawa-hada, 'pine-bark skin,' which Shiba renders here as a seaweed grain. Genuine signed Norishige are very few, so the dagger is a startlingly precious thing to find on an unknown woman.

The Saruwatari were the hereditary chief priests of the Ōkunitama Shrine, documented from the fourteenth century, so the woman is no commoner but a daughter of Fuchū's first sacerdotal house. 'Junior Fourth Rank, Lower' (jushii-no-ge) was a grade in the ancient court hierarchy, and 'Lord of Sado' an honorary title carrying no real province — marks of standing conferred on such a priest. The sister, Osae, appears to be the novelist's invention; like the heroine Oyuki later in the book, she is not a documented person.
